1.pericope_label: They journey from Elim to the wilderness of Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month, and the whole congregation murmurs against Moses and Aaron

schools.summary: Gill traces a brief halt by the Red Sea that the narrative passes over, cites a Targum for the day the Egyptian dough gave out, and excepts a few from the whole congregation; Calvin doubts that flour from Egypt was the only provision, since the country yielded fruits and herbs and the battle with Amalek suggests inhabited land nearby, and argues that the obvious remedy was prayer to a God whose particular office is to feed the hungry, so that the clamour is unbelief betraying itself.
Henry agrees on the month’s provision and its date.

Clarke takes the murmuring as proof of a degraded mind and argues that a people so carnal could never have been brought out of Egypt without striking miracles; Wesley dates the exhaustion of a month’s provision exactly and notes that the complaint fell on God’s vicegerents.

Ellicott infers long rests from a month spent in five camping-places, treats the named sites as headquarters of a host that covered a vast tract, identifies a coastal plain large enough to hold the whole congregation, and counts this the third murmuring, produced by no particular incident but by general dissatisfaction; Keil and Delitzsch argue against a rival route through the mountains, since the direct road from Elim to Sinai never touches that desert, and reject an attempt to save it by reconstruing the clause.

debates: Where the wilderness of Sin lay and by what road it was reached. Ellicott places the encampment on a broad coastal plain reached by descending to the shore, supported by the itinerary in Numbers; Keil and Delitzsch reject an inland route through the mountains as irreconcilable with a desert described as lying between Elim and Sinai, and refuse the reconstrual offered to rescue it.

What the people had lived on until now. Wesley, Henry and Gill take it as a month’s provision carried from Egypt and exactly spent; Calvin doubts this was all, and attributes the crisis to losing commerce with inhabited country as they went deeper into the desert.

3.pericope_label: Would to God we had died by the hand of the Lord in Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots and did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger

schools.summary: Gill observes that the complaint was not inward and private but spoken out, and in a very extravagant manner.

Wesley reads the wish as undervaluing the deliverance and remarks that men call whatever pain has no visible cause the pleasure of God, denies they had any great plenty in Egypt, and holds that discontent magnifies the past and vilifies the present; Clarke explains the fleshpots as the taskmasters’ boilers where slaves were fed in companies, and denies absolute want to a people who brought abundant flocks out of Egypt.

Ellicott notes that God is not named in the Hebrew and hears an allusion to the last plague in the phrase about the Lord’s hand, holds that the Israelites really had been well fed since Egyptians fed forced labourers well, and works out the arithmetic of the danger: the bulk of the cattle survived and lambs sufficed for a Passover months later, yet many had no cattle, and the desert could never have pastured herds enough to feed two million on milk and flesh; Keil and Delitzsch carry the text forward to the promise of bread from heaven.

debates: Whether the plenty they remember was real. Ellicott holds that it was, since Egyptians fed forced labourers well and the memory sharpened the want; Wesley denies it outright, making the fleshpots a product of discontent that magnifies the past.

Whether starvation was actually near. Clarke and Wesley both deny it while the flocks remained; Ellicott grants the point for the present and argues that the desert could never have supported such herds, so that the people may have foreseen the danger rather than felt it.

4.pericope_label: Then said the Lord unto Moses, Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no

schools.summary: Gill supposes Moses had been praying as usual when the people complained; Calvin reports two readings of the proving and prefers the one that binds the people by God’s bounty, holds that a rebuke must have been given and passed over in the narrative, and defends the title “bread of heaven” from the psalm while distinguishing it from the apostle’s calling the manna spiritual meat.

Clarke argues from the word “rain” that neither the substance nor the dew that produced it was native to the desert, since otherwise they would have had it for a month already; Wesley contrasts a man made of earth and fed from the earth with a people whose charters and food alike come from heaven, and states the trial as whether they will trust and be faithful.

Ellicott takes “bread from heaven” for a divine rather than merely aerial supply, renders the rate as a day’s meal each day, and makes the proving a doctrine of probation traced through Paradise, circumcision, the wilderness precepts and the Christian sacraments, all designed to test unquestioning obedience.

debates: What the proving consists in. Calvin reports one reading in which God binds the people to obedience by his own liberality and another confining the test to contentment with a day’s allowance, and prefers the first; Ellicott takes the second and widens it into a general doctrine of probation by positive precept.

5.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, that on the sixth day they shall prepare that which they bring in; and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily

schools.summary: Calvin rejects as poor the reading that confines the proving of the previous verse to sabbath observance, takes the double portion as an exception added to the promise of daily supply, and concludes that the seventh day was really hallowed before the Law was promulgated, leaving open whether the patriarchs had kept it; Gill dates the week from the first raining of bread on the first day.

Ellicott dates the sixth day from the first fall of the manna and doubts a named week existed then, since Babylonia kept a monthly sabbath without weeks and Egypt did not know the seven-day week; he prefers to read the doubled portion as an announcement of fact rather than a command, citing three scholars for a miraculous doubling.

debates: Whether the doubled portion is commanded or promised. Ellicott reports the reading that makes it an instruction to gather twice as much and prefers an announcement that what was gathered would prove to be double, a miracle rather than an order.

What the proving of the previous verse tested. Calvin reports and rejects a reading that confines it to keeping the sabbath, holding that the sabbath clause is an exception to the daily promise rather than the substance of the trial.

6.pericope_label: Moses and Aaron say that at even they shall know the Lord brought them out of Egypt, and in the morning shall see his glory, since he hears their murmurings, which are not against them but against the Lord

schools.summary: Calvin sets the announcement against the taunt of betrayal, hears a sharp reproof joined to a promise since God does not leave his work unfinished, distributes the evening to the quails and the morning to the manna, denies that the gift answered any desert, and reads “what are we?” as a refusal to be separated from God at all; Gill identifies the glory with the Shechinah, the Angel of the cloud, the eternal Word.

Clarke reads the disclaimer as the answer of servants obeying orders, notes that repeated miracles convinced only while they lasted so that a daily one was needed, and argues from the glory hearing the murmuring against the Lord that the glory is distinct from him, setting the phrase beside the apostle’s brightness of glory and express image and inferring that Christ was the visible agent in the miracles of both dispensations.

Ellicott refers the evening knowledge to the quails and the morning glory to the manna rather than to the appearance in the cloud, which preceded the quails and is nowhere placed in the morning, and finds the glory revealed in a gift that was not transient but secured the people’s subsistence for as long as they needed it.

debates: What the glory to be seen in the morning was. Ellicott refers it to the manna, on the ground that the appearance in the cloud came before the quails and is never placed in the morning; Clarke and Gill refer it to the cloud and identify it with a distinct divine agent, the Shechinah or the eternal Word.

9.pericope_label: Moses bids the congregation come near before the Lord, and as Aaron speaks the glory appears in the cloud; the Lord tells Moses they shall eat flesh at even and be filled with bread in the morning, and shall know that he is the Lord their God

schools.summary: Calvin reads the summons as a citation of criminals to a tribunal and the cloud as a presence they provoked before their eyes, presses the appearance toward the wilderness as the less habitable side, and takes the glory for something unusual meant to alarm men hardened against the ordinary manifestations; he also treats the notice that the Lord had spoken as a causal clause put last though it happened first, showing that Moses had promised nothing without command; Gill notes Aaron as spokesman and reads the message as confirming what the two had said while dealing kindly rather than resentfully.

Clarke works out what place they were summoned to, ruling out the great tabernacle as not yet built and proposing a smaller tent of meeting, and notes that the later order to lay up manna before the testimony implies a shrine already in existence or an account given here by anticipation; he prefers a simple summons to attend an extraordinary manifestation, connecting it with the promise of a thick cloud in which the people should hear and believe Moses for ever; Wesley calls the glory an extraordinary and sudden brightness and contrasts plaguing Egypt to make men know the Lord with providing for Israel to make them know their God.

Ellicott holds that though the Hebrew as pointed reads “in a cloud” the pillar of cloud is certainly meant, and that the radiance served both to rebuke the murmuring and to uphold the authority of Moses and Aaron.

debates: Where the people were told to come. Clarke rules out the great tabernacle on chronological grounds and proposes a smaller tent of meeting, while allowing that the later command about the pot of manna may mean the account is given here by anticipation.

13.pericope_label: At even the quails came up and covered the camp, and in the morning the dew lay round about the host

schools.summary: Gill traces the flight over the Arabian gulf, records a Targum that calls them pheasants and the opinion that they were locusts, and observes that here they came for one evening while later they lasted a month; Calvin makes that difference the point, since the same gift met a complaint of want here and a gluttonous craving later, and holds that a single sort was allowed so that bounds might teach dependence.

Henry distinguishes an evening feast given for delight as well as necessity, so that we may serve God cheerfully, from a morning bread given daily so that they should live on daily providence like the birds, and hears the same lesson in the petition for daily bread, adding that the plain diet teaches temperance and reporting both a tradition that the manna suited every palate and a physician’s view that so light a food was needed after their bondage.

Clarke sets out and rejects the case for locusts, since the psalm calls them flesh, the versions render a large quail, and the phrase about two cubits means two cubits apart rather than deep — had they lain three feet deep the gathering could not have taken two days — and he explains the drying in the sand as a preserving still practised, supporting the natural history from a traveller on the Egyptian netting of quails in March; Wesley notes the tameness of the birds and the daily bread that followed.

Ellicott describes the common quail’s autumn migration and the exhausted flocks dropping on the coast where they may be taken by hand, cites an ancient historian on nets spread for furlongs together, notes that the flesh is a delicacy but unwholesome in quantity, and renders the dew clause literally as a lying of dew, meaning a heavy fall.

debates: Whether the birds were quails or locusts. Clarke reports that several scholars and a bishop preferred locusts, driven by three difficulties in the text, and answers each: the psalm calls them flesh, the versions render a large quail, and the disputed measurement means distance apart rather than depth.

14.pericope_label: And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground

schools.summary: Calvin dismisses the natural identification as the idle talk of profane persons who would convict Moses of extolling a trifle, and lists the marks of miracle, an appointed hour and a supply that no frost, rain, heat or season ever interrupted; he describes the shape as dew condensed into small round grains, and Gill accounts for the dew’s disappearance by the rising sun.
Clarke observes the order of the two falls and supposes the dew was meant to cool the ground so the manna should not dissolve on landing, since the sun’s heat melted it later in the day.

Ellicott describes and rejects the two natural substances the manna has been compared with, an air-honey that comes with the dew and melts in the sun but is never found in quantity and is unfit for principal food, and an insect gum confined to particular trees, comparatively permanent and equally unfit; Keil and Delitzsch turn to the measure, a bowl a head, the tenth part of an ephah.

debates: Whether the manna can be identified with a known substance. Ellicott examines two candidates in detail and rules both out on grounds of quantity, season and unfitness for food; Calvin refuses the question as an attempt to convict Moses of extolling a trifle, and lists instead the marks that make the supply miraculous.

15.pericope_label: And when the children of Israel saw it, they said one to another, What is it? for they wist not what it was. And Moses said unto them, This is the bread which the Lord hath given you to eat

schools.summary: Calvin offers “a prepared thing” or “an assigned portion” while conceding that in Syriac and Chaldee the word is incontestably “what”, and reads the naming as a half-gratitude clouded by ignorance, since men forewarned of the miracle were astonished as though they had heard nothing, and had to be told that this was the very food promised; Gill notes they rose early to look, having been promised bread to the full.

Clarke calls the English a translation that gives no sense and contradicts itself, renders the Hebrew “what is this?” with almost all the older versions, derives the later name from the question, and argues the substance was created for the occasion, unknown to their fathers and never seen again; Wesley describes a food that came down in dew and melted yet nourished without anything else, palatable to every taste and light of digestion.

Ellicott agrees the English is certainly wrong and objects to “what is this?” as well, since the word means “what” only in Chaldee and would make a strange name, and reports four scholars for “this is a gift”, granting that the sense is Arabic rather than Hebrew though a related Hebrew verb means to give.

debates: What the name means. Clarke renders it “what is this?” with the older versions and makes the later name a memorial of the question; Ellicott rejects that as unidiomatic Hebrew and reports four scholars for “this is a gift”, while admitting the sense is Arabic; Calvin proposes two derivations of his own and concedes the Syriac and Chaldee evidence against himself.

16.pericope_label: Gather of it every man according to his eating, an omer for every man; and when they met it with an omer, he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack

schools.summary: Calvin declines the calculation as an unnecessary dispute, describes a common heap from which each took his prescribed portion so that the diligent relieved the slow without loss, and then guards the apostle’s use of the verse, since manna came daily without tillage while ordinary food requires that each possess his own, property and political government alike depending on it; Gill reads the gathering allegorically and the unequal amounts as degrees of faith.

Clarke sets out the whole Hebrew scale of capacity from the omer through the ephah, kab, homer, bath, seah, hin and log, with their derivations and English equivalents, and explains the equality naturally, as a surplus passing to households too large or too confined to gather enough in the short cool hours.

Ellicott turns the omer into arithmetic and reckons the daily supply at more than ninety thousand bushels, insists that nobody was to accumulate a store, and refuses the natural explanation of the equality, holding that a measurement always coming out at just an omer a head can only have been miraculous.

debates: How the equality was produced. Clarke and Calvin both explain it naturally, by surplus passing from the diligent to households that could not gather enough; Ellicott denies that any natural account will do, since the measure came out exactly right every time, and calls the result necessarily miraculous.

How far the apostle’s application extends. Calvin allows the parallel figuratively and refuses to let the manna’s law govern ordinary property, since society depends on each possessing his own, and reads the apostle as enjoining an equality of voluntary liberality instead.
outliers: Clarke leaves the verse to catalogue eight Hebrew measures of capacity with their etymologies and modern equivalents.

19.pericope_label: Moses says, Let no man leave of it till the morning; but some leave it and it breeds worms and stinks, and Moses is wroth; they gather it every morning, and when the sun waxes hot it melts

schools.summary: Calvin treats the hoarding as perverse unbelief in men fed as babes are fed, and their later compliance as extorted rather than voluntary, since fools are wise only after adversity; he works out how far the case governs ordinary life, allowing granaries and cellars provided the rich are liberal, unanxious and untroubled by loss, and notes that what misers gather by fraud turns to corruption in the same way; Gill guards the charge, since not all disobeyed and perhaps by far the greater part did not.

Clarke hears the petition for daily bread founded on this circumstance and reads the putrefaction as mercy in a hard form, God making disobedience irksome so that a man may find his evil ways unprofitable; Wesley pictures men sleeping quietly with no bread in the camp, and widens it into a market where hundreds of thousands were furnished without money, the same goodness bringing food yearly out of the earth as brought it daily out of the clouds.

Ellicott holds Moses must have been divinely instructed to issue the command, given so that the people should realise their absolute dependence, and argues that the breeding of worms was a penalty rather than natural decay, since no worms appeared in what was kept for the sabbath and neither natural manna decomposes rapidly; Keil and Delitzsch state the rule as taking no thought for the morrow and explain the morning gathering by the melting in the heat.

debates: Whether the corruption of the hoarded manna was natural or penal. Ellicott argues it was penal, since the sabbath portion bred no worms and no natural manna decays so fast; Clarke treats it as a divine discipline designed to make sin unprofitable.

22.pericope_label: On the sixth day they gather twice as much and the rulers tell Moses, who says, To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the Lord; and what they lay up until the morning does not stink, neither is there any worm in it

schools.summary: Calvin reads the rulers’ report as unbelief, since men who had been told plainly still marvelled at God performing what he promised, and observes that their doubting served to confirm the miracle and to give Moses occasion to enjoin a rest they might have neglected; Gill dates the sixth day from the first raining of the manna.

Henry finds a plain intimation that the sabbath was kept before Sinai and before the exodus, arguing that Moses could not have understood the double portion nor the people taken the hint without prior knowledge, and draws from the early baking a rule about arranging affairs so as not to hinder the day’s work.

Wesley reproduces Henry’s argument almost sentence for sentence; Clarke denies that anything in text or context suggests a new institution, allows that the commandment is here renewed for a people who might think themselves exempt in the wilderness, arranges the history into institution at creation, insistence at the exodus and a tenth part of the Law, and argues the miracle from a supply that failed on the seventh day and kept sweet only for it.

Ellicott answers from the Hebrew, where the article is absent both here and below, so that what is announced is a new thing; he grants a case for a primeval institution and for Babylonian observance but holds that the oppression made continuance impossible and that the elders’ surprise shows the idea was practically a novelty, and notes that baking and seething imply a substance unlike any natural manna.

debates: Whether the sabbath existed before this chapter. Henry and Wesley argue it did, from Moses understanding an unexplained command and the people taking an unexplained hint; Clarke agrees and treats the commandment as renewed rather than given; Ellicott answers that the Hebrew has no article here, so a new thing is announced, and that the oppression had made continuous observance impossible whatever may be said for a primeval institution.

25.pericope_label: Moses says, Eat that to day, for to day is a sabbath unto the Lord; six days ye shall gather it, but on the seventh there shall be none; yet some of the people go out on the seventh day to gather, and find none

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the narrative, a word spoken on the seventh morning allowing them to eat what they had in any form, and a standing rule of gathering every morning throughout their stay; Calvin calls the going out a second transgression that accused Moses of falsehood, since they credited nothing but their own eyes, and notes that the rebuke is addressed to Moses so that a general charge might fall more heavily on the multitude and lay a greater obligation on him to chastise them, hearing in “how long?” the intolerableness of a perversity that provokes new vengeance with new crimes.

Ellicott takes these words as the point at which the sabbath was instituted or re-instituted and became binding, its character as a weekly rest fixed at once by its name, by God resting from the task of giving the manna, and by the rest the absence of manna imposed, so preparing the ground for the fourth commandment.

28.pericope_label: The Lord asks how long they refuse to keep his commandments, and bids every man abide in his place on the seventh day; the people rest, and the house of Israel call the name of it manna, like coriander seed, white, and tasting like wafers made with honey

schools.summary: Gill has the Lord speaking out of the cloud, records the people’s resting without ornament, and argues from their having given it no name until now against reading the earlier verse as a naming rather than a question; Calvin takes the form as proof of miracle, the taste as proof of ingratitude, and the name itself as a testimony wrung from malicious men by the conspicuousness of the thing.

Clarke reads the command as staying home for religious exercises, reports the rabbinic limit of a thousand cubits drawn from the suburbs in Numbers, and tells two stories of literal observance carried to absurdity, a rabbi left in a slough and a man left in a pit until he died, with a dry comment on the first and a charge of murder over the second.

Ellicott counts this a second provocation, broken at least in spirit, and finds mercy in an allowance made for a new ordinance; he gives the sabbath day’s journey as six stadia, the distance from the camp’s centre to its boundary, records the extreme literalism that kept men in whatever posture they woke in but notes it was generally repudiated, corrects the Greek form of the name, and reconciles the hoar frost with the coriander seed as the manna on the ground and after collection; Keil and Delitzsch carry the command forward.

debates: How literally the command to abide in one’s place was meant. Clarke and Ellicott both report an extreme reading that kept men motionless all day, and both record the rabbinic compromise of a fixed sabbath day’s journey, though they give its length differently, Clarke at a thousand cubits from the suburbs of Numbers and Ellicott at six stadia from the centre of the camp.
outliers: Clarke leaves the verse for two mediaeval anecdotes of Jews left in a slough and a pit by Christians answering literalism with literalism.
themes: the name and taste of manna

32.pericope_label: Moses commands an omer of the manna to be filled and kept for their generations, that they may see the bread wherewith God fed them in the wilderness; and bids Aaron take a pot and lay it up before the Lord

schools.summary: Gill has Moses speaking at another time, the account inserted to keep the manna together, reviews the proposals for the pot’s material and settles on gold with the apostle, places it beside the ark rather than within, and reads the golden vessel as a figure of the word and ordinances that hold forth Christ; Calvin finds a purpose in the displaced narrative, since a memorial that never putrefied handed the miracle down, and draws from the location a lesson that God descended to their weakness by external images in order to raise them by degrees to spiritual worship.

Henry reads the memorial as evidence for a future trial, so that posterity might see the fare and the allowance and judge whether cause was ever given for murmuring, calls the preservation a standing miracle fit to memorialise miraculous food, and notes that the supply never failed a very provoking people until bread enough was in reach.
Clarke refers the reader back to his earlier note on the difficulty of a testimony that did not yet exist.

Ellicott sets “before the Lord” beside “before the Testimony”, recalls the three things the Epistle to the Hebrews places in the ark, and accounts for so sacred a deposit by the manna typifying the true bread from heaven; Keil and Delitzsch derive the word for the vessel from a root meaning to preserve, so a jar and not a basket, and note that the Greek supplies an adjective for gold with nothing answering to it in the Hebrew.

debates: What the pot was made of. Gill reports earthen, brass and glass among the proposals and settles the question by the Greek version and the apostle’s word for gold; Keil and Delitzsch note the same divergence and observe that the adjective for gold has nothing answering to it in the Hebrew.

34.pericope_label: Aaron lays it up before the Testimony to be kept; the children of Israel eat manna forty years until they come to the borders of Canaan; and an omer is the tenth part of an ephah

schools.summary: Gill places the pot beside the ark and explains the name of the testimony from the law it contained, reckons the forty years as forty less thirty days from one passover to another, and uses the closing measure to show how ample the provision was, giving both the rabbinic scale in eggshells and a modern conversion into gallons and quarts.

Clarke notes that the Testimony belonged to a tabernacle not yet built and takes the word to signify reference beyond itself, answers the argument that the book must postdate the manna by attributing the verse to Ezra as collector and arranger of the canon, says the closing note on the omer belongs several verses earlier, and closes on the type, that salvation is of the Lord and the manna figured the Redeemer as Christ himself applied it; Wesley works the typology out at length, Christ the true manna, the word the manna that nourishes and the Spirit’s comforts the hidden manna, gathered by each for himself, sufficient without superfluity, and contrasted with a food whose eaters hungered again and died.

Ellicott keeps the verse about the forty years for Moses, written shortly before his death when the manna had run thirty-nine years and nine months, and notes that it does not say the supply had ceased, as in fact it did not until Jordan was crossed; he explains the final gloss by the omer being an Egyptian measure that fell out of use early while the ephah lasted until the captivity, so the note may have been added by a later editor.

debates: Who wrote the notice of the forty years. Clarke reports its use as an argument that Exodus postdates the manna and attributes the sentence to Ezra as arranger of the canon; Ellicott keeps it for Moses himself, written near the end of the forty years and not implying that the supply had stopped.
